decks.title: Ratio Analysis — Part 1: Liquidity and Solvency Ratios, and Effects of Transactions
goals: State how ratios are expressed and name the four groups of ratios in the ISC syllabus
Compute and interpret the current ratio and the quick ratio using the Schedule III heads
Compute and interpret the debt to equity, proprietary, debt to total assets and interest coverage ratios
Work out whether a transaction increases, decreases or leaves unchanged the current, quick or debt-equity ratio
Find missing figures from given liquidity ratios

slides.heading: Ratio Analysis
slides.body_md: Part 1 — what ratios are, the **liquidity** and **solvency** ratios of an imagined company, and how transactions move them.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: what a ratio is, the four groups, current and quick ratios, effects of transactions on them, solvency ratios, effects on the debt-equity ratio and missing figures
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: A balance sheet tells us that current liabilities are five lakh rupees. Is that a lot? We cannot say until we set it against what the company holds to pay them. Ratio analysis sets related figures side by side. In this part we meet the four groups of ratios, work out the liquidity and solvency ratios of an imagined company, Mohiniyattam Coir, and see how single transactions move three key ratios.

slides.heading: What is a ratio?
bullets: A ratio relates **two figures** from the financial statements.
**Ratio analysis**: computing, comparing and interpreting ratios.

visual.alt: Table of the forms in which ratios are expressed: a pure ratio such as two to one, times such as ten times, a percentage such as twenty-five per cent, and rupees per share such as three rupees of earnings per share
visual.caption: Rounding rule in this chapter: two decimal places, rounded half up.

slides.narration: A ratio is a relationship between two related figures from the financial statements. It may be written as a pure ratio, such as a current ratio of two to one; in times, such as inventory turnover of ten times; as a percentage, such as a gross profit ratio of twenty-five per cent; or in rupees per share, such as earnings per share of three rupees. We round every ratio to two decimal places.

slides.heading: The four groups in the syllabus

rows: Can short-term dues be paid on time?
Is the long-term financial structure safe?
Debt to equity; proprietary; debt to total assets; interest coverage
Trade receivables, trade payables, inventory and working capital turnover
How much does the business earn?
Gross profit, net profit, operating, operating profit ratios; earnings per share; price-earnings; return on investment

visual.alt: Table of the four groups of ratios in the syllabus: liquidity, solvency, activity and profitability, with the question each answers and the ratios in each

slides.narration: Your syllabus groups ratios into four families. Liquidity ratios ask whether short-term dues can be paid. Solvency ratios ask whether the long-term structure is safe. Activity, or turnover, ratios ask how efficiently resources are used. Profitability ratios ask how much the business earns, and they include earnings per share, the price-earnings ratio and return on investment.

slides.heading: Quick check: sort the ratios
slides.body_md: Match each ratio with its group.
slides.narration: For each ratio, ask which question it answers: paying short-term dues, long-term safety, efficiency, or earnings.

slides.heading: Our case company: Mohiniyattam Coir Ltd

visual.alt: Condensed balance sheet of Mohiniyattam Coir as at 31 March 2026 in the Schedule Three order: shareholders' funds 18,00,000, non-current liabilities 7,20,000, current liabilities 5,00,000; non-current assets 20,20,000, current assets 10,00,000; total 30,20,000
visual.caption: An imagined company; sub-head totals only.

slides.narration: Meet Mohiniyattam Coir, an imagined company in Vaikom. Its balance sheet, in the Schedule Three order, totals rupees thirty lakh twenty thousand. Shareholders' funds are rupees eighteen lakh, long-term debt rupees seven lakh twenty thousand and current liabilities rupees five lakh. Current assets are rupees ten lakh. We will work out every ratio in this chapter from these figures and its statement of profit and loss.

slides.heading: Liquidity: the current ratio
bullets: Around **2 : 1** is the traditional comfort level.
Too low: dues may not be met. Too high: idle cash, slow stock or slow collection.

rows: Other current liabilities (outstanding expenses, unpaid dividends)
Short-term loans and advances; prepaid expenses and other current assets

visual.alt: Table of what goes into the current ratio under the Schedule Three heads: current investments, inventories, trade receivables, cash, short-term loans and advances and prepaid expenses, over short-term borrowings, trade payables, other current liabilities and short-term provisions
visual.caption: Current ratio = current assets ÷ current liabilities; conventional level 2 : 1.

slides.narration: The current ratio divides current assets by current liabilities, taken from the Schedule Three heads. Current assets are current investments, inventories, trade receivables, cash, short-term loans and advances and prepaid expenses. Current liabilities are short-term borrowings, trade payables, other current liabilities and short-term provisions. Two to one is the traditional comfort level, but very high is not always good.

slides.heading: Liquidity: the quick ratio

rows: Inventories: must be sold first, and perhaps on credit
Prepaid expenses: never come back as cash

visual.alt: Table of quick assets: cash, trade receivables, current investments and short-term loans are kept; inventories and prepaid expenses are taken out
visual.caption: Quick ratio = quick assets ÷ current liabilities; conventional level 1 : 1.

slides.narration: The quick ratio, also called the liquid or acid-test ratio, is a sharper test. From current assets we remove inventories, which must first be sold, and prepaid expenses, which never come back as cash. What remains, quick assets, is divided by current liabilities. One to one is the usual benchmark: every rupee due soon is covered by a rupee that is almost cash.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: liquidity of Mohiniyattam Coir
slides.body_md: Mohiniyattam Coir (imagined): current assets ₹10,00,000, of which inventories ₹4,00,000 and prepaid expenses ₹20,000; current liabilities ₹5,00,000.

visual.alt: Working for the liquidity ratios of Mohiniyattam Coir: current assets 10,00,000, quick assets 5,80,000, current liabilities 5,00,000; current ratio two to one, quick ratio one point one six to one

slides.narration: Current assets of rupees ten lakh over current liabilities of rupees five lakh give a current ratio of two to one. Taking out inventories and prepaid expenses leaves quick assets of rupees five lakh eighty thousand, so the quick ratio is one point one six to one. Both meet the usual benchmarks: Mohiniyattam can pay its short-term dues without waiting to sell its coir stock.

slides.heading: Quick check: quick assets
slides.narration: Besides inventories, which current asset will never turn back into cash?

slides.heading: How a transaction moves a ratio
bullets: Recompute with the **new** figures; never guess.
The rules depend on whether the ratio is above or below 1.

rows: Raises both parts by the same amount
Lowers both parts by the same amount
Raises only the numerator, or lowers only the denominator
Lowers only the numerator, or raises only the denominator
Swaps one item for another inside the same part

visual.alt: Table of rules for the effect of a transaction on a ratio: an equal rise in both parts lowers a ratio above one, an equal fall raises it, a change in one part moves the ratio in that direction, and a swap within one part changes nothing
visual.caption: Rules follow from the arithmetic; always recompute to confirm.

slides.narration: A transaction can change the numerator, the denominator, both or neither. When both parts rise by the same amount, a ratio above one falls, and when both fall by the same amount, it rises. A change in one part alone moves the ratio the same way. A swap inside one part, such as collecting cash from a debtor, changes nothing. Always confirm by recomputing.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: five transactions, two ratios
slides.body_md: Mohiniyattam Coir (imagined): each transaction is taken separately, starting from current assets ₹10,00,000, quick assets ₹5,80,000 and current liabilities ₹5,00,000.

rows: (ii) Buys coir yarn for ₹50,000 in cash
(iii) Buys coir yarn on credit for ₹1,00,000
(iv) Sells mats costing ₹40,000 for ₹50,000 in cash

visual.alt: Table of five separate transactions of Mohiniyattam Coir and their effect on its current and quick ratios: paying creditors raises both, buying yarn for cash leaves the current ratio unchanged but lowers the quick ratio, buying yarn on credit lowers both, selling mats at a profit for cash raises both, and a long-term loan raises both
visual.caption: Each transaction is taken separately from the starting figures.

slides.narration: Paying creditors lowers both parts and raises both ratios. Buying yarn for cash leaves the current ratio at two to one but lowers the quick ratio, because cash becomes stock. Buying yarn on credit lowers both. Selling mats at a profit for cash raises both. A long-term loan brings cash in with no current liability, so both ratios rise.

slides.heading: Quick check: which leaves it unchanged?
slides.body_md: Choose the transaction that leaves the current ratio as it is.
slides.narration: Look for a transaction that swaps one current asset for another.

slides.heading: Solvency ratios

rows: more reliance on borrowed long-term funds: riskier for lenders
owners finance more of the assets: safer for outsiders
more of the assets financed by long-term debt: riskier
Profit before interest and tax ÷ Interest on long-term debt
interest is easier to pay out of profit

visual.alt: Table of the four solvency ratios with their formulas and what a higher figure means: debt to equity, proprietary, debt to total assets and interest coverage
visual.caption: Debt = long-term borrowings + long-term provisions; equity = shareholders' funds.

slides.narration: Solvency ratios look at the long term. Debt means long-term borrowings plus long-term provisions; equity means shareholders' funds. The debt to equity ratio compares the two. The proprietary ratio shows the share of total assets financed by owners, and debt to total assets the share financed by long-term debt. Interest coverage asks how many times profit before interest and tax covers the interest on long-term debt.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: solvency of Mohiniyattam Coir
slides.body_md: Mohiniyattam Coir (imagined): share capital ₹13,50,000, reserves and surplus ₹4,50,000, 10% debentures ₹6,00,000, long-term provisions ₹1,20,000, total assets ₹30,20,000; profit before interest and tax ₹5,60,000.

rows: 5,60,000 ÷ 60,000 ≈ 9.33 times (profit before interest and tax over interest on debentures)

visual.alt: Working for the solvency ratios of Mohiniyattam Coir: debt 7,20,000, equity 18,00,000, total assets 30,20,000; debt to equity zero point four to one, debt to total assets zero point two four to one, proprietary zero point six to one, interest coverage nine point three three times

slides.narration: Debt of rupees seven lakh twenty thousand against equity of rupees eighteen lakh gives a debt to equity ratio of zero point four to one. Measured against total assets, debt gives zero point two four to one and equity gives zero point six to one, after rounding. Profit before interest and tax of rupees five lakh sixty thousand covers the debenture interest of rupees sixty thousand about nine point three three times. Lenders are well protected.

slides.heading: How a transaction moves the debt-equity ratio

rows: (i) Issues equity shares for ₹2,00,000 in cash
(iv) Issues bonus shares of ₹3,00,000 from the general reserve

visual.alt: Table of five separate transactions of Mohiniyattam Coir and their effect on its debt to equity ratio of zero point four to one: a share issue lowers it, a long-term loan raises it, redeeming debentures lowers it, a bonus issue leaves it unchanged and paying a dividend raises it
visual.caption: Starting point: 7,20,000 ÷ 18,00,000 = 0.4 : 1.

slides.narration: Start from Mohiniyattam's debt to equity ratio of zero point four to one. A share issue for cash raises equity, so the ratio falls. A new long-term loan raises debt, so it rises. Redeeming debentures lowers debt. A bonus issue moves money from a reserve to share capital, both inside shareholders' funds, so nothing changes. Paying a dividend reduces equity, so the ratio rises.

slides.heading: Quick check: a share issue
slides.narration: Ask which part of the debt to equity ratio a share issue changes.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: missing liquidity figures
slides.body_md: An imagined company, **Gotipua Brassware Ltd**, Pipili, has a current ratio of 3 : 1, a quick ratio of 1.8 : 1, working capital of ₹4,00,000 and prepaid expenses of ₹20,000. Find its current liabilities, current assets, quick assets and inventories.

rows: Working capital is (3 − 1) times the current liabilities
Inventories = current assets − quick assets − prepaid expenses

visual.alt: Steps for worked example four: working capital of 4,00,000 is twice the current liabilities, so current liabilities are 2,00,000, current assets 6,00,000, quick assets 3,60,000 and inventories 2,20,000

slides.narration: Sometimes the ratios are given and the figures are missing. With a current ratio of three to one, working capital is twice the current liabilities, so current liabilities are rupees two lakh and current assets rupees six lakh. The quick ratio gives quick assets of rupees three lakh sixty thousand. Inventories are what is left after quick assets and prepaid expenses: rupees two lakh twenty thousand. Recomputing both ratios confirms the answers.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Profit before interest and tax ÷ Interest on long-term debt

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: formulas of the current, quick, debt to equity, debt to total assets, proprietary and interest coverage ratios with the values for Mohiniyattam Coir

slides.narration: To sum up: ratios relate two figures and are written as a proportion, in times, as a percentage or in rupees per share. Liquidity ratios compare current or quick assets with current liabilities. Solvency ratios compare long-term debt with equity and with total assets, equity with total assets, and profit before interest and tax with interest. Recompute both parts to see how a transaction moves a ratio.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Write **formula → working → answer**; each carries marks.
State the result in the right form: **x : 1**, **times**, **%** or **₹ per share**, to two decimal places.
Show **quick assets**, **debt** and **equity** as separate workings.
For a transaction, write the **new figures** and the **new ratio**, then say increase, decrease or no change.
Missing figures: build each step from a ratio, then **recompute** the given ratios as a check.
slides.narration: In the examination, write the formula, then the working, then the answer in the right form, rounded to two decimal places. Show quick assets, debt and equity as separate workings. For a transaction, write the new figures and the new ratio before you say whether it rises or falls. When you find missing figures, recompute the given ratios to check.

decks.title: Ratio Analysis — Part 2: Activity and Profitability Ratios
goals: Compute trade receivables, trade payables, inventory and working capital turnover ratios using averages and credit figures
Find the cost of revenue from operations and average inventory from given figures
Compute the gross profit, net profit, operating and operating profit ratios, separating operating from non-operating items
Compute earnings per share, the price-earnings ratio, capital employed and return on investment
Find missing figures from given ratios and read a set of ratios together

slides.heading: Activity and profitability ratios
slides.body_md: Part 2 — **turnover** ratios, **profitability** ratios including earnings per share and price-earnings, and **return on investment**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: turnover ratios, cost of revenue and averages, the operating statement and its ratios, earnings per share and price-earnings, capital employed and return on investment, missing figures and reading ratios together
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: In part one we asked whether a company can pay its debts. Now we ask how well it uses its resources and how much it earns. Turnover ratios count how many times receivables, payables, inventory and working capital turn over in a year. Profitability ratios measure profit against revenue, per share and against capital employed. We continue with Mohiniyattam Coir.

slides.heading: Activity ratios in the syllabus

visual.alt: Table of the four turnover ratios in the syllabus, each a flow of the year over a resource: trade receivables, trade payables, inventory and working capital turnover
visual.caption: All in times. Average = (opening + closing) ÷ 2.

slides.narration: Each activity ratio sets a flow of the year against the resource behind it. Trade receivables turnover uses credit revenue over average receivables, which include bills receivable. Trade payables turnover uses net credit purchases over average payables. Inventory turnover uses the cost of revenue from operations over average inventory. Working capital turnover uses revenue from operations over working capital. Each is stated in times.

slides.heading: Cost of revenue from operations and average inventory

visual.alt: Working of the cost of revenue from operations of Mohiniyattam Coir: opening inventory plus purchases plus direct expenses less closing inventory gives 37,50,000, which is also revenue less gross profit; average inventory 3,75,000

slides.narration: Inventory is valued at cost, so inventory turnover uses the cost of revenue from operations. For Mohiniyattam, opening inventory plus purchases plus direct expenses, less closing inventory, gives rupees thirty-seven lakh fifty thousand, which equals revenue less gross profit. Average inventory is the opening and closing figures added and halved: rupees three lakh seventy-five thousand.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: three turnover ratios
slides.body_md: Mohiniyattam Coir (imagined): credit revenue ₹42,00,000; net credit purchases ₹30,00,000; trade receivables ₹3,60,000 at the start and ₹4,40,000 at the end of the year; trade payables ₹2,00,000 and ₹3,00,000.

visual.alt: Working for the inventory, trade receivables and trade payables turnover of Mohiniyattam Coir: ten times, ten point five times and twelve times
visual.caption: Credit revenue ₹42,00,000; credit purchases ₹30,00,000.

slides.narration: Mohiniyattam's inventory turned over ten times. Credit revenue of rupees forty-two lakh against average receivables of rupees four lakh gives ten point five times. Credit purchases of rupees thirty lakh against average payables of rupees two lakh fifty thousand give twelve times. So it pays its suppliers a little faster than its customers pay it, which is worth watching.

slides.heading: Quick check: inventory turnover
slides.narration: Average the two inventory figures first, then divide the cost of revenue by that average.

slides.heading: Working capital turnover

rows: Each rupee of working capital supports ten rupees of revenue
Compare with last year and with similar firms

visual.alt: Working capital turnover of Mohiniyattam Coir: working capital 5,00,000, revenue 50,00,000, turnover ten times

slides.narration: Working capital is current assets less current liabilities: for Mohiniyattam, rupees five lakh. Revenue from operations of rupees fifty lakh is ten times that working capital. A rising figure means each rupee of working capital is supporting more revenue, but a very high one may mean working capital is too thin for safety.

slides.heading: Profitability: the operating statement

rows: Less: Cost of revenue from operations
Less: Loss on sale of furniture

visual.alt: Operating statement of Mohiniyattam Coir: revenue 50,00,000, gross profit 12,50,000, operating profit 5,50,000, profit before interest and tax 5,60,000, profit before tax 5,00,000 and profit after tax 3,75,000
visual.caption: Interest received and the loss on sale of furniture are non-operating.

slides.narration: Profitability ratios are measured on revenue from operations. Mohiniyattam's gross profit is rupees twelve lakh fifty thousand. Taking away operating expenses leaves an operating profit of rupees five lakh fifty thousand. Non-operating items, such as interest received and a loss on selling furniture, come next, giving profit before interest and tax. Then debenture interest and tax leave a profit after tax of rupees three lakh seventy-five thousand.

visual.caption: Segment widths are computed from the operating statement.

slides.narration: Think of every hundred rupees of revenue. For Mohiniyattam, seventy-five rupees go on the cost of revenue and fourteen rupees on operating expenses, an operating ratio of eighty-nine per cent. The eleven rupees left are operating profit, so the operating profit ratio is eleven per cent. The two always add up to one hundred.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: gross, operating and net profit ratios
slides.body_md: Mohiniyattam Coir (imagined): revenue from operations ₹50,00,000; gross profit ₹12,50,000; operating cost ₹44,50,000; operating profit ₹5,50,000; profit after tax ₹3,75,000.

visual.alt: Working for the profitability ratios of Mohiniyattam Coir: gross profit twenty-five per cent, operating ratio eighty-nine per cent, operating profit ratio eleven per cent, net profit ratio seven point five per cent

slides.narration: Mohiniyattam's gross profit ratio is twenty-five per cent. Its operating ratio is eighty-nine per cent and its operating profit ratio eleven per cent. The net profit ratio, on profit after tax, is seven point five per cent. The gap between operating profit and net profit is made up of non-operating items, debenture interest and tax.

slides.heading: Quick check: operating ratio
slides.narration: Add the operating expenses to the cost of revenue, then divide by revenue and multiply by one hundred.

slides.heading: Earnings per share and the price-earnings ratio

rows: From the Statement of Profit and Loss (after interest and tax)
Rate × preference share capital, for the year
Equity share capital ÷ face value of one share
Market price per equity share ÷ earnings per share, in times

visual.alt: Table of the steps for earnings per share and the price-earnings ratio: profit after tax, less preference dividend, divided by the number of equity shares, then market price divided by earnings per share

slides.narration: Earnings per share shows the profit earned for each equity share. Start from profit after tax, take out the preference dividend, and divide by the number of equity shares. The price-earnings ratio then divides the market price of a share by its earnings per share. It tells us how many rupees investors are paying for each rupee of yearly earnings.

slides.heading: Worked example 7: earnings per share and price-earnings
slides.body_md: Mohiniyattam Coir (imagined): profit after tax ₹3,75,000; 10% preference shares ₹1,50,000; 1,20,000 equity shares of ₹10 each; market price ₹36.

visual.alt: Working for the earnings per share and price-earnings ratio of Mohiniyattam Coir: earnings for equity shareholders 3,60,000 over 1,20,000 shares gives three rupees; a market price of thirty-six rupees gives a price-earnings ratio of twelve times

slides.narration: Mohiniyattam's preference dividend is rupees fifteen thousand, leaving rupees three lakh sixty thousand for equity shareholders. Spread over one lakh twenty thousand shares, that is earnings per share of three rupees. With the share selling at thirty-six rupees, the price-earnings ratio is twelve times.

slides.heading: Quick check: earnings per share
slides.narration: Earnings per share is worked out for one kind of share only. Which?

slides.heading: Capital employed: three routes, one answer

visual.alt: Capital employed of Mohiniyattam Coir worked out three ways: shareholders' funds plus non-current liabilities, non-current assets plus working capital, and total assets less current liabilities, all give 25,20,000
visual.caption: The routes must agree; if they do not, an item has been misplaced.

slides.narration: Capital employed is the long-term money in the business. From the liabilities side it is shareholders' funds plus non-current liabilities: for Mohiniyattam, rupees twenty-five lakh twenty thousand. From the assets side it is non-current assets plus working capital, and total assets less current liabilities gives it a third time. All three must agree.

slides.heading: Worked example 8: return on investment
slides.body_md: Mohiniyattam Coir (imagined): profit before tax ₹5,00,000 after debenture interest of ₹60,000; capital employed ₹25,20,000.

visual.alt: Working for the return on investment of Mohiniyattam Coir: profit before interest and tax 5,60,000 on capital employed 25,20,000 gives twenty-two point two two per cent, well above the ten per cent it pays on its debentures

slides.narration: Return on investment uses profit before interest and tax, because capital employed includes the lenders' money. For Mohiniyattam that profit is rupees five lakh sixty thousand. Divided by capital employed of rupees twenty-five lakh twenty thousand, it gives twenty-two point two two per cent, well above the ten per cent it pays on its debentures.

slides.heading: Quick check: capital employed
slides.narration: From the assets side, what is added to the non-current assets?

slides.heading: Worked example 9: missing profitability figures
slides.body_md: An imagined company, **Kathak Attar Ltd**, Jaunpur, has a price-earnings ratio of 15, a share price of ₹45, 2,00,000 equity shares, a preference dividend of ₹40,000 and a net profit ratio of 8%. Find its earnings per share, profit after tax and revenue from operations.

rows: Earnings per share = market price ÷ price-earnings ratio
Profit after tax = earnings + preference dividend
Revenue from operations = profit after tax ÷ net profit ratio

visual.alt: Steps for worked example nine: a market price of forty-five rupees and a price-earnings ratio of fifteen give earnings per share of three rupees, earnings of 6,00,000, profit after tax of 6,40,000 and revenue of 80,00,000

slides.narration: Work backwards. Earnings per share is the price, forty-five rupees, divided by the price-earnings ratio of fifteen: three rupees. Times two lakh shares, earnings are rupees six lakh; adding the preference dividend gives a profit after tax of rupees six lakh forty thousand. At a net profit ratio of eight per cent, revenue is rupees eighty lakh.

slides.heading: Reading the ratios together

rows: Can pay current dues without selling stock
Pays suppliers a little faster than customers pay it
Long-term funds earn more than they cost

visual.alt: Interpretation table for Mohiniyattam Coir: liquidity meets the conventions, borrowing is modest and interest well covered, customers pay a little more slowly than the company pays suppliers, and return on investment is well above the cost of its debentures
visual.caption: A ratio means something only against a benchmark, a past year or similar firms.

slides.narration: A ratio means something only when it is compared: with a benchmark, a past year or similar firms. Mohiniyattam meets the liquidity benchmarks, borrows modestly and covers its interest comfortably. Its customers pay a little more slowly than it pays its suppliers, and its long-term funds earn more than they cost. Read the four groups together before you judge.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 2

rows: Credit revenue from operations ÷ Average trade receivables
Net credit purchases ÷ Average trade payables
Cost of revenue from operations ÷ Average inventory
Profit after tax ÷ Revenue from operations × 100
(Cost of revenue from operations + Operating expenses) ÷ Revenue from operations × 100

sections.heading: 1. Ratio analysis and the four ISC groups
sections.body_md:
An **accounting ratio** expresses the relationship between two related figures in the financial statements, for example current assets and current liabilities. **Ratio analysis** means computing such ratios, comparing them (with past years, other firms or accepted standards) and interpreting them.

**Forms:** pure ratio (2 : 1); times (10 times); percentage (25%); rupees per share (₹3.00).

**The ISC syllabus lists four groups:**
- **Liquidity:** current ratio; quick (liquid or acid-test) ratio.
- **Solvency:** debt to equity; proprietary; debt to total assets; interest coverage.
- **Activity:** trade receivables, trade payables, inventory and working capital turnover.
- **Profitability:** gross profit, net profit, operating and operating profit ratios; earnings per share; price-earnings ratio; return on investment.

Ratios are read by comparison: with a convention (2 : 1, 1 : 1), with the same firm last year, or with similar firms.

**Definitions.** The first table fixes every base used in the chapter; the second lists all seventeen formulas. Points to note:
- Current assets and current liabilities follow the **Schedule III** heads of the balance sheet.
- **Debt** means non-current liabilities only; current liabilities never enter the solvency ratios.
- **Capital employed** can be reached three ways (liabilities side, assets side, total assets − current liabilities); the answers must agree.
- Inventory, receivables and payables turnover use **averages** of opening and closing figures; working capital turnover uses the **year-end** working capital. If only closing figures are given, use them; if credit figures are not given, use the totals.

**Rounding rule.** Work every ratio to **two decimal places**, rounded half up (0.9625 → 0.96; 10.125 → 10.13); an exact result is written as it is (2.5 : 1, 25%). Earnings per share is written in rupees and paise (₹2.30).

sections.heading: 3. Liquidity ratios
sections.body_md:
**Current ratio = current assets ÷ current liabilities.** Conventional level **2 : 1**. Below 1 : 1, current liabilities exceed current assets and dues may not be met; a very high ratio suggests idle cash, excess stock or slow collection.

**Quick (liquid or acid-test) ratio = quick assets ÷ current liabilities**, where quick assets = current assets − inventories − prepaid expenses. Conventional level **1 : 1**. It tests whether short-term dues can be paid without selling stock, which is why a banker often prefers it when much of the current assets is slow-moving inventory.

**Watch the items:** bills receivable belong to trade receivables; a bank overdraft is a short-term borrowing (current liability); debentures, long-term loans and long-term provisions are non-current.

sections.heading: 4. Solvency ratios
sections.body_md:
**Debt to equity ratio = debt ÷ equity** (debt = long-term borrowings + long-term provisions; equity = shareholders' funds). Lower means a larger safety margin for lenders and a smaller fixed interest burden.

**Proprietary ratio = shareholders' funds ÷ total assets.** The share of the assets financed by owners; higher is safer for outsiders.

**Debt to total assets ratio = debt ÷ total assets.** The share of the assets financed by long-term debt; lower is safer.

**Interest coverage ratio = profit before interest and tax ÷ interest on long-term debt** (times). How many times the interest is earned; a high figure means interest will be paid even if profit falls. Work back to profit before interest and tax: profit after tax → add tax → add interest.

sections.heading: 5. Effects of transactions on the current, quick and debt-equity ratios
sections.body_md:
**Method.** For each transaction (taken separately): (1) write the change in the numerator and the denominator; (2) recompute the ratio; (3) compare with the original and state **increase, decrease or no change**.

**Rules that follow from the arithmetic** (see the table):
- an equal **rise** in both parts **lowers** a ratio above 1; an equal **fall** **raises** it (the opposite for a ratio below 1);
- a change in one part only moves the ratio in that direction;
- a swap inside one part changes nothing (collecting a debtor: current ratio unchanged).

**Typical cases.** Buying inventory for cash: current ratio unchanged, quick ratio falls. Buying inventory on credit: both fall (when above 1). Issuing shares for cash: liquidity ratios rise, debt-equity falls. Redeeming debentures in cash: debt-equity falls. Bonus shares from reserves: debt-equity unchanged. Paying a dividend: debt-equity rises.

*Not in the ISC 2027 syllabus:* effect-of-transaction problems on ratios other than the current, quick and debt-equity ratios.

sections.heading: 6. Activity (turnover) ratios
sections.body_md:
- **Trade receivables turnover = credit revenue from operations ÷ average trade receivables** (debtors + bills receivable). Higher means faster collection.
- **Trade payables turnover = net credit purchases ÷ average trade payables** (creditors + bills payable). Lower means the firm takes longer to pay; a sudden fall may signal a cash strain.
- **Inventory turnover = cost of revenue from operations ÷ average inventory.** Higher means faster-moving stock; very high may mean too little stock.
- **Working capital turnover = revenue from operations ÷ working capital.**

**Finding cost of revenue:** opening inventory + net purchases + direct expenses (wages, carriage inwards) − closing inventory; or revenue − gross profit. If gross profit is a percentage **on cost**, cost = revenue × 100 ÷ (100 + rate). Revenue from operations is net of sales returns; purchases are net of purchases returns.

sections.heading: 7. Profitability ratios, earnings per share and return on investment
sections.body_md:
- **Gross profit ratio = gross profit ÷ revenue from operations × 100.**
- **Net profit ratio = profit after tax ÷ revenue from operations × 100.**
- **Operating ratio = (cost of revenue from operations + operating expenses) ÷ revenue from operations × 100.**
- **Operating profit ratio = operating profit ÷ revenue from operations × 100 = 100 − operating ratio.**
- **Earnings per share = (profit after tax − preference dividend) ÷ number of equity shares.** Number of shares = equity share capital ÷ face value.
- **Price-earnings ratio = market price per equity share ÷ earnings per share** (times).
- **Return on investment = profit before interest and tax ÷ capital employed × 100.**

Operating ratios ignore non-operating items (interest or dividend received, profit or loss on sale of assets, loss by fire) and finance costs; the net profit ratio includes them. Return on investment uses profit **before** interest because capital employed includes the lenders’ money; compare it with the rate of interest the company pays.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Using **revenue** instead of **cost of revenue from operations** in inventory turnover, or closing instead of **average** inventory.
- Leaving **bills receivable / bills payable** out of trade receivables and payables, or using total instead of **credit** figures.
- Putting **current liabilities** into debt, or forgetting **long-term provisions**.
- Forgetting **prepaid expenses** when working out quick assets.
- Including **non-operating** items or interest in the operating ratio.
- Using profit after tax in **return on investment** or **interest coverage** (both need profit before interest and tax).
- In earnings per share, ignoring the **preference dividend** or dividing by rupees of capital instead of the **number** of equity shares.
- Guessing the effect of a transaction instead of **recomputing** the ratio.
- Writing the answer in the wrong form (25 instead of 25%, 2 instead of 2 : 1) or not rounding to two decimal places.

**How marks are usually split (Ratio Analysis carries 8 marks in Section B)**
- 1 mark: one ratio, one formula or one effect in an objective item.
- 2 marks: a pair of ratios, or two transaction effects (1 mark each).
- 3 marks: three ratios (about 1 mark each, formula and working counted), or a short missing-figure chain.
- 5 marks: a question in parts, for example bases and ratios 2 + ratios and comment 3.
- 8 marks: a full problem of six to eight ratios from the statements, or a long missing-figure chain.

questions.stem_md: Kalbelia Camel Leather Ltd, an imagined company in Lunkaransar, has a quick ratio of 1.4 : 1. Its quick assets are ₹2,10,000 and its inventories ₹1,20,000; it has no prepaid expenses. Find its current liabilities, its current assets and its current ratio.

questions.stem_md: Most of the current assets of an imagined company, Jhumair Pickles Ltd, Khunti, are jars of pickle in its godown, some of which take many months to sell. Explain why its banker may rely more on its quick ratio than on its current ratio.
questions.solution_md: Two points: why inventory weakens the current ratio as a test, and what the quick ratio measures instead.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Inventory is the least liquid current asset.** Jhumair’s pickles must first be sold, perhaps on credit, before they bring in cash; slow-moving stock may not be saleable at book value at all. The current ratio counts it in full, so it can look comfortable even when cash is short.
2. **The quick ratio is a sharper test.** It compares only cash, receivables and similar assets (current assets less inventories and prepaid expenses) with current liabilities, so it shows whether the dues can be met without waiting for the stock to sell. A banker lending short-term wants that assurance.

marking_scheme.step: Inventory slow to convert; inflates the current ratio
Quick ratio tests payment without relying on stock

questions.stem_md: Dandiya Lacquer Toys Ltd, an imagined company in Sankheda, has a current ratio of 2.75 : 1 and working capital of ₹3,50,000. Its inventories are ₹2,40,000 and its prepaid expenses ₹10,000. Find its current liabilities, its current assets and its quick ratio.

questions.stem_md: The proprietary ratio of an imagined company, Karakattam Brass Pots Ltd, Aruppukottai, is 0.75 : 1. This tells its lenders that

three-quarters of its total assets are current assets

questions.stem_md: Kolattam Wooden Toys Ltd, an imagined company in Proddatur, has a 9% long-term loan of ₹8,00,000, outstanding for the whole year. Its profit after tax is ₹3,78,000, and tax is 30% of profit before tax. Its interest coverage ratio is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** 8.5 times. Profit before tax = 3,78,000 × 100 ÷ 70 = 5,40,000; interest = 72,000; profit before interest and tax = 6,12,000. Coverage = 6,12,000 ÷ 72,000 = 8.5 times.

questions.stem_md: Two imagined coffee estates are compared by a bank: Huttari Coffee Estates Ltd, Virajpet, covers its debenture interest 2 times, and a rival covers its interest 10 times. What does this suggest about Huttari?

Its current assets are only twice its current liabilities

questions.stem_md: Mardani Forgings Ltd, an imagined company in Kagal, publishes its interest coverage ratio in its annual report. Which group of readers is most directly concerned with that ratio?

The workers in its forge shop
Holders of its debentures and its long-term lenders

questions.stem_md: Tillana Copperware Ltd, an imagined company in Amroha, has: equity share capital ₹10,00,000; reserves and surplus ₹5,00,000; long-term borrowings ₹5,00,000; long-term provisions ₹1,00,000; trade payables ₹3,00,000; short-term provisions ₹1,00,000; property, plant and equipment ₹16,00,000; non-current investments ₹1,00,000; inventories ₹4,00,000; trade receivables ₹2,50,000; cash and cash equivalents ₹1,50,000. answer.model_answer_md:
Total assets = 16,00,000 + 1,00,000 + 4,00,000 + 2,50,000 + 1,50,000 = 25,00,000 (equal to the total of equity and liabilities). Shareholders' funds = 10,00,000 + 5,00,000 = 15,00,000; debt = 5,00,000 + 1,00,000 = 6,00,000.

questions.stem_md: Tandava Steel Utensils Ltd, an imagined company in Jagadhri, had 10% debentures of ₹6,00,000 and a 12% long-term bank loan of ₹2,50,000, both outstanding for the whole year. Its profit after charging this interest but before tax was ₹3,90,000. Calculate its interest coverage ratio.

- Profit before interest and tax = 3,90,000 + 90,000 = 4,80,000.
- Interest coverage ratio = Profit before interest and tax ÷ Interest on long-term debt = 4,80,000 ÷ 90,000 ≈ 5.33 times.

questions.stem_md: An investor is thinking of buying debentures of an imagined company, Oppana Teak Furniture Ltd, Malappuram. Explain what each of these three ratios of the company would tell her: (a) debt-equity ratio, (b) proprietary ratio, (c) interest coverage ratio.
questions.solution_md: For each ratio: what it compares, and whether a higher or lower figure is safer for a debenture holder.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a) Debt-equity ratio** (long-term debt ÷ shareholders' funds) shows how far the company depends on borrowed long-term funds. A low ratio means owners have put in most of the long-term money, so her claim is well protected; a high ratio means heavy borrowing and a large fixed interest burden.

**(b) Proprietary ratio** (shareholders' funds ÷ total assets) shows what share of the assets the owners have financed. The higher it is, the larger the cushion of owners' money behind outside lenders if the assets ever had to be sold.

**(c) Interest coverage ratio** (profit before interest and tax ÷ interest on long-term debt) shows how many times the yearly interest is earned. A high figure means her interest is likely to be paid even if profits fall.

questions.stem_md: An imagined sweet-maker, Nritta Sweets Ltd, Mandya, is comparing its inventory turnover ratio with that of other sweet-makers. State what (a) a very high and (b) a very low inventory turnover ratio may indicate about its stock.

**(b) Very low:** stock is moving slowly: too much has been made or bought, some may be stale or unsaleable, and money that could earn elsewhere is tied up in the godown.

questions.stem_md: The accountant of an imagined company, Dekhni Shellcraft Ltd, Mapusa, reports both an operating ratio and an operating profit ratio. Distinguish between the two ratios and state how they are related.
questions.solution_md: Give each formula with what it shows, then the link between them.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Operating ratio:** operating cost (the cost of revenue from operations together with the operating expenses) expressed as a percentage of revenue from operations. For Dekhni it shows how much of each rupee of revenue is used up in making and selling its shell articles; a lower figure is better.

**Operating profit ratio:** operating profit (gross profit less operating expenses) expressed as a percentage of revenue from operations. It shows how much of each rupee of revenue is left as profit from the main business; a higher figure is better.

**Relation:** both are measured on the same base, and operating cost plus operating profit makes up the whole of that revenue, so the two percentages always total 100.

marking_scheme.step: The two ratios add up to 100 per cent

questions.stem_md: A retired teacher holds equity shares of an imagined company, Wangala Pineapple Ltd, Williamnagar. Explain what (a) earnings per share, (b) the price-earnings ratio and (c) return on investment tell her about the company.
questions.solution_md: One mark for each ratio: what it measures and how an equity shareholder reads it.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a) Earnings per share** (profit after tax less preference dividend, per equity share) shows how much the company has earned for each of her shares in the year, whether or not it is paid out as dividend. Rising earnings per share points to a growing business.

**(b) Price-earnings ratio** (market price per share ÷ earnings per share) shows how many rupees the market pays for each rupee of yearly earnings. A high figure means investors expect earnings to grow, or that the share is costly; compared with similar companies it helps her judge whether to hold or sell.

**(c) Return on investment** (profit before interest and tax ÷ capital employed × 100) shows how well the management uses all the long-term funds in the business. If it is higher than the rate of interest the company pays, borrowing adds to what is left for shareholders.

| (i) Purchased goods for ₹40,000 in cash | No change | No change | 6,00,000 ÷ 2,40,000 = 2.5 : 1 | **No change** |
| (ii) Issued debentures for ₹1,20,000 in cash | +1,20,000 | No change | 7,20,000 ÷ 2,40,000 = 3 : 1 | **Increases** |

Reasons: (i) cash, a current asset, is replaced by inventory, another current asset, so neither part moves; (ii) cash comes in from a long-term source, so current assets rise while current liabilities do not.

questions.stem_md:
Ghumura Stoneware Ltd, an imagined company in Bhawanipatna, has long-term debt of ₹6,00,000 and shareholders' funds of ₹15,00,000. Taking each transaction separately, state with a reason its effect on the debt-equity ratio and show the new ratio:

(i) Redeemed debentures of ₹1,50,000 in cash.
(ii) Issued bonus shares of ₹3,00,000 out of the general reserve.
questions.solution_md: Ask whether each transaction changes long-term debt, shareholders’ funds as a whole, both or neither.

answer.model_answer_md:
Debt-equity ratio before = 6,00,000 ÷ 15,00,000 = 0.4 : 1.

| Transaction | Change in debt | Change in equity | New ratio | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| (i) Redeemed debentures of ₹1,50,000 in cash | −1,50,000 | No change | 4,50,000 ÷ 15,00,000 = 0.3 : 1 | **Decreases** |
| (ii) Issued bonus shares of ₹3,00,000 out of the general reserve | No change | No change | 6,00,000 ÷ 15,00,000 = 0.4 : 1 | **No change** |

Reasons: (i) debt falls and equity is unchanged (the cash paid out is not part of equity); (ii) the bonus issue moves 3,00,000 from the general reserve to share capital, both inside shareholders' funds, so equity as a whole does not change.

questions.stem_md:
Nongkrem Turmeric Ltd, an imagined company in Jowai, has quick assets of ₹3,60,000 and current liabilities of ₹3,00,000. Taking each transaction separately, state with a reason whether its quick ratio increases, decreases or does not change, and show the new ratio:

(i) Purchased goods for ₹60,000 in cash.
(ii) Paid trade payables ₹1,00,000.
(iii) Sold goods costing ₹40,000 on credit for ₹50,000.
questions.solution_md: For the quick ratio, inventory never counts: follow only cash, receivables and current liabilities.

answer.model_answer_md:
Quick ratio before = 3,60,000 ÷ 3,00,000 = 1.2 : 1.

| Transaction | Change in quick assets | Change in current liabilities | New ratio | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| (i) Purchased goods for ₹60,000 in cash | −60,000 | No change | 3,00,000 ÷ 3,00,000 = 1 : 1 | **Decreases** |
| (ii) Paid trade payables ₹1,00,000 | −1,00,000 | −1,00,000 | 2,60,000 ÷ 2,00,000 = 1.3 : 1 | **Increases** |
| (iii) Sold goods costing ₹40,000 on credit for ₹50,000 | +50,000 | No change | 4,10,000 ÷ 3,00,000 ≈ 1.37 : 1 | **Increases** |

Reasons: (i) cash, a quick asset, turns into inventory, which is not; (ii) both parts fall by the same amount, and with the ratio above 1 that raises it; (iii) the goods leave inventory (not quick) at cost, but the debtor of 50,000 is a quick asset, so quick assets rise by the full sale price.

questions.stem_md:
Ponung Orange Growers Ltd, an imagined company in Dambuk, has current assets of ₹5,00,000 (of which quick assets ₹3,00,000), current liabilities of ₹2,50,000, long-term debt of ₹4,00,000 and shareholders' funds of ₹10,00,000. Taking each transaction separately, show its effect on the current ratio, the quick ratio and the debt-equity ratio:

(i) Issued equity shares for ₹2,00,000 in cash.
(ii) Bought a sorting machine for ₹50,000, payable in six months.
(iii) Raised a long-term loan of ₹1,00,000 in cash.
questions.solution_md: For each transaction list the change in current assets, quick assets, current liabilities, debt and equity, then recompute all three ratios.

answer.model_answer_md:
Before: current ratio 5,00,000 ÷ 2,50,000 = 2 : 1; quick ratio 3,00,000 ÷ 2,50,000 = 1.2 : 1; debt-equity 4,00,000 ÷ 10,00,000 = 0.4 : 1.

| Transaction | Current ratio | Quick ratio | Debt-equity ratio |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| (i) Issued equity shares for ₹2,00,000 in cash | 7,00,000 ÷ 2,50,000 = 2.8 : 1: **Increases** | 5,00,000 ÷ 2,50,000 = 2 : 1: **Increases** | 4,00,000 ÷ 12,00,000 ≈ 0.33 : 1: **Decreases** |
| (ii) Bought a sorting machine for ₹50,000, payable in six months | 5,00,000 ÷ 3,00,000 ≈ 1.67 : 1: **Decreases** | 3,00,000 ÷ 3,00,000 = 1 : 1: **Decreases** | 4,00,000 ÷ 10,00,000 = 0.4 : 1: **No change** |
| (iii) Raised a long-term loan of ₹1,00,000 in cash | 6,00,000 ÷ 2,50,000 = 2.4 : 1: **Increases** | 4,00,000 ÷ 2,50,000 = 1.6 : 1: **Increases** | 5,00,000 ÷ 10,00,000 = 0.5 : 1: **Increases** |

(i) Cash (current and quick) and equity rise; debt is unchanged. (ii) The amount owed for the machine is a current liability; cash does not move and the machine is a non-current asset, so debt and equity are untouched. (iii) Cash and long-term debt both rise.

questions.stem_md:
Tarangamel Barge Services Ltd, an imagined company in Mormugao, has long-term debt of ₹9,00,000 and shareholders' funds of ₹18,00,000.

(a) Calculate its debt-equity ratio. [1]

(b) Taking each transaction separately, state whether its debt-equity ratio increases, decreases or does not change, giving the new ratio: [4]

(i) Issued 12% debentures of ₹3,00,000 for cash.
(ii) Redeemed preference shares of ₹2,00,000 at par in cash, out of profits.
(iii) Paid an interim dividend of ₹90,000.
(iv) Issued equity shares of ₹4,00,000 to the vendor of a building.
questions.solution_md: Ask of each transaction whether it moves long-term debt, shareholders’ funds as a whole, or both; transfers between reserves and capital do not move equity.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Debt-equity ratio = Debt ÷ Equity (shareholders' funds) = 9,00,000 ÷ 18,00,000 = 0.5 : 1.

**(b)**

| Transaction | Change in debt | Change in equity | New ratio | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| (i) Issued 12% debentures of ₹3,00,000 for cash | +3,00,000 | No change | 12,00,000 ÷ 18,00,000 ≈ 0.67 : 1 | **Increases** |
| (ii) Redeemed preference shares of ₹2,00,000 at par in cash, out of profits | No change | −2,00,000 | 9,00,000 ÷ 16,00,000 ≈ 0.56 : 1 | **Increases** |
| (iii) Paid an interim dividend of ₹90,000 | No change | −90,000 | 9,00,000 ÷ 17,10,000 ≈ 0.53 : 1 | **Increases** |
| (iv) Issued equity shares of ₹4,00,000 to the vendor of a building | No change | +4,00,000 | 9,00,000 ÷ 22,00,000 ≈ 0.41 : 1 | **Decreases** |

Reasons: (i) only long-term debt rises; (ii) share capital is paid off in cash (the transfer from profits to the capital redemption reserve stays inside shareholders' funds), so equity falls by 2,00,000; (iii) the dividend is paid out of the surplus, so equity falls; (iv) the building is paid for with new shares, so equity rises and debt is unchanged.

questions.stem_md:
Dumhal Saffron Ltd, an imagined company in Pampore, has these current items on 31 March 2026:

| Particulars | ₹ |
| --- | ---: |
| Inventories | 1,80,000 |
| Trade receivables | 1,50,000 |
| Cash and cash equivalents | 90,000 |
| Prepaid expenses | 20,000 |
| Trade payables | 1,60,000 |
| Outstanding expenses | 40,000 |

(a) Calculate its current ratio and quick ratio. [2]

(b) Taking each transaction separately, show its effect on both ratios: [3]

(i) Paid trade payables ₹40,000.
(ii) Bought saffron stock for ₹30,000 in cash.
(iii) Wrote off a bad debt of ₹10,000.
questions.solution_md: Fix the base figures first; for each transaction change current assets, quick assets and current liabilities, then recompute both ratios.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Current assets = 4,40,000; quick assets = 4,40,000 − 1,80,000 − 20,000 = 2,40,000; current liabilities = 2,00,000. Current ratio = 4,40,000 ÷ 2,00,000 = 2.2 : 1; quick ratio = 2,40,000 ÷ 2,00,000 = 1.2 : 1.

**(b)**

| Transaction | Current ratio | Quick ratio |
| --- | --- | --- |
| (i) Paid trade payables ₹40,000 | 4,00,000 ÷ 1,60,000 = 2.5 : 1: **Increases** | 2,00,000 ÷ 1,60,000 = 1.25 : 1: **Increases** |
| (ii) Bought saffron stock for ₹30,000 in cash | 4,40,000 ÷ 2,00,000 = 2.2 : 1: **No change** | 2,10,000 ÷ 2,00,000 = 1.05 : 1: **Decreases** |
| (iii) Wrote off a bad debt of ₹10,000 | 4,30,000 ÷ 2,00,000 = 2.15 : 1: **Decreases** | 2,30,000 ÷ 2,00,000 = 1.15 : 1: **Decreases** |

(i) Both parts of each ratio fall by the same amount, and both ratios are above 1, so both rise. (ii) Cash becomes inventory: total current assets do not change, but quick assets fall. (iii) Trade receivables, a current and quick asset, fall with no change in liabilities.

questions.stem_md:
From the following information about Mathuri Chilli Traders Ltd, an imagined company in Byadgi, find (a) its current liabilities and current assets, (b) its closing inventory, (c) its opening and average inventory, (d) its cost of revenue from operations and (e) its revenue from operations.

- Working capital ₹3,00,000; current ratio 2.5 : 1; quick ratio 1.3 : 1; no prepaid expenses.
- Inventory turnover ratio 8 times; opening inventory was ₹40,000 less than closing inventory.
- Gross profit is 25% on cost.
questions.solution_md: Work as a chain: working capital and the current ratio give both totals; the quick ratio isolates inventory; turnover gives cost; the margin on cost gives revenue.

questions.stem_md:
Kathakali Pepper Exports Ltd, an imagined company in Thalassery, gives the following for the year ended 31 March 2026: revenue from operations ₹90,00,000 (credit ₹72,00,000); opening inventory ₹5,00,000; purchases ₹65,00,000; direct expenses ₹3,00,000; employee benefits expense ₹7,00,000; depreciation and amortisation ₹4,00,000; other operating expenses ₹3,00,000; interest received on non-current investments ₹40,000; loss on sale of furniture ₹40,000; interest on debentures for the full year; tax at 25% of profit before tax. Trade receivables on 1 April 2025 were ₹4,00,000. Its condensed balance sheet as at 31 March 2026 is:

| Particulars | 31 March 2026 (₹) |
| --- | ---: |
| **I. Equity and Liabilities** |   |
| **Shareholders' funds** |   |
|   Share capital (equity shares of ₹10 each) | 30,00,000 |
|   Reserves and surplus | 12,00,000 |
| **Non-current liabilities** |   |
|   10% Debentures | 12,00,000 |
|   Long-term provisions | 2,00,000 |
| **Current liabilities** |   |
|   Trade payables | 5,00,000 |
|   Other current liabilities | 1,00,000 |
|   Short-term provisions | 2,00,000 |
| **Total** | **64,00,000** |
| **II. Assets** |   |
| **Non-current assets** |   |
|   Property, plant and equipment (net) | 40,00,000 |
|   Intangible assets | 2,00,000 |
|   10% Non-current investments | 4,00,000 |
| **Current assets** |   |
|   Current investments | 1,00,000 |
|   Inventories | 7,00,000 |
|   Trade receivables | 6,00,000 |
|   Cash and cash equivalents | 3,60,000 |
|   Prepaid expenses | 40,000 |
| **Total** | **64,00,000** |

Calculate: (a) current ratio, (b) quick ratio, (c) debt-equity ratio, (d) interest coverage ratio, (e) inventory turnover ratio, (f) trade receivables turnover ratio, (g) operating ratio and (h) return on investment.
questions.solution_md: Build the operating statement and the bases (quick assets, debt, averages, capital employed) before computing; each ratio is then one line.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Operating statement**

| Particulars | ₹ |
| --- | ---: |
| Revenue from operations | 90,00,000 |
| Less: Cost of revenue from operations | (66,00,000) |
| **Gross profit** | **24,00,000** |
| Less: Employee benefits expense | (7,00,000) |
| Less: Depreciation and amortisation | (4,00,000) |
| Less: Other operating expenses | (3,00,000) |
| **Operating profit** | **10,00,000** |
| Add: Interest on non-current investments | 40,000 |
| Less: Loss on sale of furniture | (40,000) |
| **Profit before interest and tax** | **10,00,000** |
| Less: Interest on long-term debt | (1,20,000) |
| **Profit before tax** | **8,80,000** |
| Less: Tax at 25% | (2,20,000) |
| **Profit after tax** | **6,60,000** |

Cost of revenue from operations = 5,00,000 + 65,00,000 + 3,00,000 − 7,00,000 = 66,00,000; average inventory = 6,00,000. Quick assets = 18,00,000 − 7,00,000 − 40,000 = 10,60,000. Debt = 12,00,000 + 2,00,000 = 14,00,000. Average trade receivables = 5,00,000. Capital employed = 42,00,000 + 14,00,000 = 56,00,000 (= 46,00,000 + 10,00,000).

| Ratio | Formula | Working | Result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| (a) Current ratio | Current assets ÷ Current liabilities | 18,00,000 ÷ 8,00,000 = 2.25 : 1 | **2.25 : 1** |
| (b) Quick ratio | Quick assets ÷ Current liabilities | 10,60,000 ÷ 8,00,000 ≈ 1.33 : 1 | **1.33 : 1** |
| (c) Debt-equity ratio | Debt ÷ Equity (shareholders' funds) | 14,00,000 ÷ 42,00,000 ≈ 0.33 : 1 | **0.33 : 1** |
| (d) Interest coverage ratio | Profit before interest and tax ÷ Interest on long-term debt | 10,00,000 ÷ 1,20,000 ≈ 8.33 times | **8.33 times** |
| (e) Inventory turnover ratio | Cost of revenue from operations ÷ Average inventory | 66,00,000 ÷ 6,00,000 = 11 times | **11 times** |
| (f) Trade receivables turnover ratio | Credit revenue from operations ÷ Average trade receivables | 72,00,000 ÷ 5,00,000 = 14.4 times | **14.4 times** |
| (g) Operating ratio | (Cost of revenue from operations + Operating expenses) ÷ Revenue from operations × 100 | 80,00,000 ÷ 90,00,000 × 100 ≈ 88.89% | **88.89%** |
| (h) Return on investment | Profit before interest and tax ÷ Capital employed × 100 | 10,00,000 ÷ 56,00,000 × 100 ≈ 17.86% | **17.86%** |
